The health economics support the program. Prevention that pays, in the Netherlands, public health economics for alcohol policy.
plos-pone-0005796: Variant CJD risk hinges on prion gene variants. Segarra and colleagues studied prion protein processing in blood cells and the codon 129 polymorphism. The work informs vCJD susceptibility. Blood cells' prion biology, genotyped, M/M homozygosity's deadly link, BSE's human legacy.
plos-pone-0006396: DNA walks hide mirror patterns. Poptsova and team found hidden mirror in DNA walks of 671 DNA bundles. Machine flips restore order — genomes' secret mirrors, found by shuffles. Germs neat, humans messy, from half-turns to static, with gene order flipped in silico.
plos-pone-0006496: Melioidosis needs a vaccine. Hara and team flagged immune-waking surface proteins of Burkholderia pseudomallei. The targets await shot design — a germ's vaccine hopes, mapped, where no shot exists. Endemic regions, high death toll: surface proteins weighed, use unknown, bets picked.
plos-pone-0006596: Anemic fish hearts grow two ways. Sun and team found zebrafish hearts enlarge by cell growth and cell gain in anemia. The heart rebuilds itself — fish hearts' double fix, mapped, with high regrowth. Push-pull stress, myocyte question: reshaping studied, adult fish.
plos-pone-0009396: Malaria risk can swing wildly between villages just a few miles apart, because mosquito breeding grounds vary street by street. This study builds fine-grained habitat maps of the mosquitoes that carry malaria across northern Tanzania. By matching satellite and field data to where the insects thrive, the models help health officials aim bed nets and spraying exactly where they'll save the most lives.
plos-pone-0009496: Red blood cell precursors are usually harvested by mobilizing bone marrow — an invasive step. This paper shows they can be grown directly from ordinary blood draws, without mobilization or pre-sorting, and still function properly. The method simplifies research on blood diseases and on parvovirus, which infects exactly these cells.
plos-pone-0009596: Anthrax spores linger in Central Asian soil for decades. This study models where Bacillus anthracis could thrive in Kazakhstan under different climate futures. The paper gives health planners a map of a persistent threat, showing how a warming world may redraw anthrax country.
plos-pone-0010396: Barn owls hunt by sound, weighing different frequency cues. This study finds a dominance hierarchy among the cues they use to locate prey. The paper reveals how a master hunter's brain ranks its senses when signals conflict. The ranking reveals a brain that triages sound the way a pilot triages instruments.
plos-pone-0010496: Brain inflammation suppresses the birth of new neurons. This study finds the algae spirulina protects neural stem cells from inflammation-driven decline. The paper tests a natural supplement as a brain-cell guardian. The result adds a natural ally to the brain-repair toolkit.
plos-pone-0010596: Brain cells grow elaborate branches — and the transcription factor Cux1 shapes them. This study shows Cux1 controls dendrite form in cortical pyramidal neurons. The paper reveals a sculptor of the brain's wiring. The finding links a single gene to the shape of thought itself.
plos-pone-0010696: Kidney cancer's most common form needs better markers. This study defines a pathway signature and differentiation program in clear cell renal carcinoma. The paper profiles the disease's biology. The signature could one day guide therapy choices for kidney cancer patients worldwide.
plos-pone-0010796: Our cells stash fat in droplets — with molecular help. This study reveals structural insights into how the FIT2 protein mediates triglyceride storage. The paper exposes the fat-stashing machinery. The structure informs research on obesity and metabolic disease. The machinery is a future drug target.
plos-pone-0010896: Pregnant women were feared especially vulnerable to 2009 H1N1. This register-based cohort study on the island of La Réunion found a surprisingly low clinical burden in pregnancy. The paper delivers reassuring island data. The findings calm maternal-health planning. The island's experience defied global fears.
plos-pone-0010996: Causal diagrams are everywhere in science — comparing them needs math. This paper develops statistical tests for associations between two directed acyclic graphs. The methods let researchers compare causal networks rigorously. The toolkit serves data science. The tests bring rigor to network comparison.
plos-pone-0011096: Bees fit themselves to the places they live. This study looks at how honey bee groups adjust to local weather and food. The paper maps bee change. The finding helps beekeepers and wild-bee protection. The map helps bees weather our changing world.
plos-pone-0011196: Testing live badgers for tuberculosis is notoriously tricky. This study compares the diagnostic accuracy of three TB tests in live badgers and finds the optimal way to use them. The paper guides wildlife disease management. The finding helps control bovine TB spread.
plos-pone-0011296: Multiple sclerosis risk genes reach beyond the usual suspect. This study finds a major histocompatibility complex class I locus contributes to MS susceptibility independently from HLA-DRB1*15:01. The paper reveals added genetic risk. The finding informs neurogenetics. The informed genetics refines risk prediction.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1296:
On 16 July 1945, the day before Potsdam opened, the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Staff papers like this one did the thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The chiefs' eve-of-summit notes formed the base of the brief the team carried to Germany.

Writing before the talks let the staff state its view cleanly, untouched by the day's trades. Later papers would bend with events. This one holds the starting line. It is part of the groundwork stack of 16 July, the day the American machine finished its Potsdam preparations on paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1396:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, wrote to Georges Bidault, the French foreign minister, on 31 July 1945. The volume prints six Caffery letters to Bidault from the turn of August 1945. It is the second of two Caffery letters to Bidault dated that day.

Two letters in one day suggest either two subjects or one subject that would not wait. Bidault had taken France's foreign policy in hand after liberation. He dealt with Caffery as the voice of the power whose aid France most needed. Readers should read this letter with its twin. Together they show the range of Franco-American business, from the grand settlement in Germany down to the daily needs of a freed but battered country.
frus-1945-50-intel-d96:
Magruder answered McCloy on 9 October 1945. The SSU chief reported to the assistant secretary who served as his unit's chief defender in the War Department. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Replies in this thread show Magruder accounting for his command: its people, its stations, and its shrinking funds. The SSU still ran secret work abroad that no other American body could yet do, and Magruder's letters pressed that fact politely and often. Readers can follow the exchange month by month as the unit's fate hung between abolition and absorption. Each letter bought time, and time, for the SSU, was the whole game.
frus-1945-50-intel-d196:
On 13 June 1946, the General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Group (Houston) sent a memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). It is document 196 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d296:
Commander Robert Jay Williams addressed a memorandum to the Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Cassady) on 23 July 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 296 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d396:
J. Prichard Childs, chief of the CIA staff for intelligence planning, wrote to the members of the IAC Standing Committee on 25 August 1949. The memo is document 396 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Intelligence Advisory Committee, or IAC, joined the CIA with the intelligence chiefs of the State Department and the armed services. Its standing committee did the ground work between full meetings. A memo to that group shows how shared views were built, step by step, before they reached the top. The committee's work rarely made news, yet it shaped the joint reports the President saw.
frus-1861-d96:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 October 1861. The letter is document 96 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Lyons letters in three days point to business that would not wait. The autumn mails carried claims and protests in both directions. His second note shows the British envoy pressing his points while the ink on the first was barely dry. Claims by British merchants, whose goods the blockade had seized, drove much of this pace. Seized goods and halted ships filled the claim books of both governments that fall.
frus-1861-d196:
John Appleton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 May 1861. The dispatch is document 196 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton wrote as Clay drew near to take over the Russian post. His late spring reports kept the file warm through the change of men. The letter shows a handover done with care, in a capital where good will was a real asset. Care in a handover is a small virtue that this file shows more than once. Care of that kind kept the Russian goodwill safe through the change of men.
frus-1861-d296:
24 August 1861 brought Mr. Harvey a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 296 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d96:
Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 9 July 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 96 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d196:
On 11 December 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, in a note printed as Document 196 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The two men were the working channel between their governments.

Mid-December 1861 found the Trent crisis at its peak, with Britain demanding the release of the seized Confederate envoys and an apology. Washington had not yet answered. A note exchanged in those days belonged to the most delicate fortnight in Anglo-American dealings during the whole war, when a second conflict seemed possible. Lyons also reported home on each note, so most of these papers exist in two archives.
frus-1862-d296:
Filed as Document 296 but dated 11 July 1862, this report from William L. Dayton in Paris went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The printers placed it after a later Seward dispatch in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Dayton wrote while Europe absorbed the news of McClellan's retreat, which made the Union look weaker than it had in spring. His reading of the French response mattered greatly in Washington. The letter's date, not its number, fixes its place: the anxious second week of July 1862. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d396:
Bayard Taylor, at the American legation in St. Petersburg, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 November 1862. It is Document 396 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs. That series is the State Department record laid before Congress with the President's annual message.

Instructions like this one carried Washington's line to its men abroad and told them what to say at foreign courts. In late 1862 the Union still feared that Britain or France might back the Confederacy. A friendly Russia mattered more each month. The dispatch shows Seward working to hold that friendship fast while the war ground on at home.
frus-1862-d496:
The same day Pike's own report was dated at The Hague, 16 April 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to him. It is Document 496 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Crossed letters like these two show the machinery of the system: Washington sent orders based on month-old reports, while ministers acted on judgment between orders. Seward's April instruction to The Hague dealt with the standing Dutch subjects, from neutrality rules to the war's presentation in the Dutch press. Pike answered in his own blunt fashion in due course. The pair of letters, read together, gives a fair picture of how distant the two ends of the correspondence really were.
frus-1862-d596:
On 28 July 1862 Thomas Corwin reported from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 596 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Corwin's late-July report closed the summer's first run of Mexican papers in the volume. The French were in the country to stay, the republic was fighting on, and the United States was reduced to watching with sympathy. His letters from these months gave the State Department its fullest picture of the invasion as Mexicans experienced it. They also fixed the American record for the future. A victorious Union would one day return to the question of a French-backed empire. It would face that question on its border with very different strength.
frus-1862-d696: On 19 June 1862, a letter went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to a Mr. Crosby. The letter is document 696 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering Crosby's dispatch of the month before. The record gives the two names and the date, but not Crosby's post or the subject of the exchange. It is described here only at that level.
frus-1863p1-d96:
On 27 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 96 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, closing the legation's February mail in the file.

A month-end letter often took stock. Adams's February had run from the Queen's speech to a flood of late-month sheets, and this one rounds the set off. His reports gave Washington a clear, cool read on the power it most feared and most needed. The dispatch is a fitting last page for the month in a file that rarely missed a week.
frus-1863p1-d196:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 9 May 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 196 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d296: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 19 September 1863. It is document 296 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d396:
Washington's business with Britain on 20 February 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 396 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Notes on this route often dealt with single ships, single cargoes, or single men. Small cases mattered, because each one tested what neutrality would allow. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d496:
7 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d596:
Dated 25 July 1863, document 596 is a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020096:
Hajime Hirase, Lifen Qian, Peter Barthó, and their team imaged living brain support cells for PLOS Biology in 2004. Astrocytes are star-shaped cells that support neurons. They signal with waves of calcium, and the team watched those waves move through networks of astrocytes in living animals.

Seeing the waves in an intact brain, rather than in a dish, shows how they really spread and sync. Calcium waves may help astrocytes coordinate blood flow and neuron support across a wide area. The work pushes imaging methods forward as well. It gives researchers a way to watch non-neuron brain cells at work in real time, a view that was long out of reach.
plos-pbio-0020196:
Michèle Crozatier, Jean-Michel Ubeda, Alain Vincent, and their team studied fly immunity in PLOS Biology in 2004. When a wasp lays an egg inside a fruit fly larva, the larva must surround it with blood cells and kill it. That defense is called encapsulation.

A gene named collier, the fly version of a family of early B-cell factors, proves vital for the response. Without it, the larva cannot mount the cell attack properly. The study links a gene known from vertebrate blood development to an insect defense, hinting at deep shared roots. It also gives immunity research a clean genetic handle on how blood cells are called into action.
plos-pbio-0020296:
Matt Kaeberlein, Kathryn T. Kirkland, Stanley Fields, and their team tested an aging theory in yeast in PLOS Biology in 2004. Cutting food intake extends life in many species, an effect called calorie restriction. In yeast, the gene Sir2 was thought to be the required middleman for that benefit.

The team found yeast can live longer on less food even without Sir2. So the pathway forks: Sir2 helps in some settings but is not the only route. That result kept the field honest about a tidy story. It pushed aging research to map several paths from diet to lifespan, a map that remains central to work on healthy aging.
plos-pone-0000096:
Yuuki Hayashi, Takuyo Aita, Hitoshi Toyota, and their team charted a protein fitness landscape by experiment in PLOS ONE in 2006. A fitness landscape maps how each change in a protein's sequence affects how well it works. Theory draws these maps as hills and valleys, but real ones are hard to measure.

By making many variants of one protein and testing each, the team drew a real section of such a map. It proved rugged: small steps could help, harm, or do nothing, in no simple pattern. Rugged maps explain why protein evolution can get stuck at local peaks. Measured landscapes like this one ground a famous theory in laboratory fact.
plos-pone-0000196:
Evangelos Evangelou, Demetrius M. Maraganore, and John P. A. Ioannidis published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome-wide association studies scan the whole genome for disease links, and meta-analysis pools many such studies for stronger evidence. The authors lay out strategies for doing that pooling well, applying them to Parkinson disease.

Single studies of gene effects are often too small to trust. A sound meta-analysis can separate real signals from chance hits. The paper gives practical guidance on combining genome-wide datasets and shows it at work on Parkinson's, where genetic clues have been hard to pin down.
plos-pone-0000296:
Nick J. B. Isaac, Samuel T. Turvey, Ben Collen, and colleagues published this conservation paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The EDGE approach ranks species by combining how threatened they are with how phylogenetically distinct they are, how much unique evolutionary history they carry. The authors apply it to mammals, setting conservation priorities on both grounds.

A species like the aardvark holds a whole branch of the mammal family tree. Losing it loses more history than losing one of many similar rodents. The paper lists which mammals score highest on threat plus distinctness. It gives conservation a defensible way to spend limited funds.
plos-pone-0000396:
Wei Zhang and colleagues hunted for DNA letter changes tied to where a gene is switched on, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes make UGT1A enzymes, which help the body process drugs and its own chemicals, and different family members work in different tissues. The team searched for single-letter variants linked to those tissue-specific expression patterns.

A variant that changes where an enzyme is made can change how a person handles a drug. That makes this search part of pharmacogenetics, the study of how inherited differences shape drug response. Cataloging such variants is a step toward dosing medicines by a patient's genes rather than by averages.
plos-pone-0000496:
Antonio Graziano and colleagues improved stem cell bone building with a pitted surface, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. They grew stem cell-derived osteoblasts, bone-forming cells, on scaffold surfaces containing concave pits. The shaped surfaces improved the cells' performance and led to significant bone tissue formation.

Cells read the geometry of what they sit on: pits of the right size can nudge stem cells to become bone and lay down mineral. For regenerative medicine, the scaffold is half the therapy. A surface design that boosts bone formation could serve in implants for fractures and jaw work. Growing real bone there beats filling gaps with inert material.
plos-pone-0000596:
Thomas Karrasch and colleagues reported a warning about a plant compound often assumed to be protective, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Luteolin is a flavonoid found in vegetables and supplements. The team used NF-κB EGFP transgenic mice. These mice glow where the inflammation switch NF-κB is active. In them, the flavonoid luteolin worsened chemical-induced colitis. It did so by blocking NF-κB-dependent protective molecules.

NF-κB drives inflammation but also protects the gut lining; blocking it can backfire. The reporter mice made that double role visible in living tissue. The paper cautions against assuming natural antioxidants are safe in inflamed organs, and it refines where anti-inflammatory drugs should and should not act.
plos-pone-0000696:
Alexander Zumdieck, Karsten Kruse, Henrik Bringmann and colleagues gave a physical analysis of the ring that splits a cell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. During cytokinesis, a contractile ring of actin filaments squeezes the cell into two. The authors analyze how stress builds in that ring and how its filaments turn over, constantly replaced while the ring shrinks.

Their case study is the embryo of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, a classic model. They present a general analysis of force balances and material exchange in the ring. Physics of this kind matters because division errors drive disease. A ring that both contracts and renews itself is an engineering puzzle worth solving exactly.
plos-pone-0000796:
Morten Nielsen, Claus Lundegaard, Thomas Blicher and colleagues presented NetMHCpan, a predictor for a core step in immune recognition, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Binding of peptides to MHC molecules is the single most selective step when the cellular immune system recognizes pathogens. The human MHC class I system, HLA-I, is extremely polymorphic, with a huge and growing registry of variants.

Older predictors handled only specific HLA types. NetMHCpan aims at any HLA-A and HLA-B protein of known sequence, giving quantitative binding predictions. Pan-specific prediction matters for vaccine design across diverse populations. A peptide vaccine must bind the HLA variants real people carry. Binding only the common laboratory ones is not enough.
plos-pone-0000896:
Jon Beadell, Colm Atkins, Erin Cashion and colleagues compared immune traits in four island bird groups, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hawaii's native birds have been hit hard by bird malaria and pox brought in by people. With fewer parasites around and smaller gene pools, island birds might share a changed immune profile.

The team measured immune signals across four island taxa and found they do not all point the same way. That divergence is itself the lesson: a parasite poor home does not reshape every species alike. For conservation, the work warns against treating island birds as one uniform case.
plos-pone-0000996:
Isabel Miranda, Rita Rocha, Maria Santos and colleagues showed that a changed genetic code creates variety in a human pathogen, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genetic code was once thought frozen and universal. Found exceptions in bacteria and eukaryotes alike ended that idea, showing codon assignments can shift.

Candida albicans, a fungus that infects people, reads one codon in an unusual way. The team argue this alteration acts as a phenotype diversity generator, producing varied cell surfaces and traits from one genome. Variety helps a pathogen dodge immunity and drugs. A code quirk once treated as a curiosity here becomes a survival strategy.
plos-pone-0001096:
Meei Ling Sheu, Shing Hwa Liu and Keng Hsin Lan tested a plant compound against gastric cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Honokiol is a small natural product from magnolia, reported to fight tumors and the blood vessels that feed them. Its molecular mechanisms, and whether it works against gastric cancer, were unknown.

The team report honokiol induces cleavage of a stress protein, GRP94, through calpain enzymes, and triggers apoptosis, ordered cell death, in human gastric cancer cells. It also reduced tumor growth in their model. Natural products often fail for lack of a mechanism; here the mechanism is the headline. Gastric cancer remains hard to treat, so new routes matter.
plos-pone-0001196:
Insulin affects the brain as well as the body, raising activity in the cerebral cortex of lean people. Otto Tschritter and colleagues tested a long-acting insulin, detemir, in overweight people, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. In obese individuals the brain's response to insulin is reduced, a sign of cerebrocortical insulin resistance.

The authors asked whether insulin detemir is a suitable tool to restore the cerebral insulin response in overweight humans. They tracked cerebrocortical beta activity, a rhythm of brain electrical activity that insulin stimulates. Their work bears on how brain insulin resistance might be reversed, with implications for appetite and weight control.
plos-pone-0001296:
Flu seasons differ around the world, but the global pattern had never been fully described for each virus type. Brian Finkelman and colleagues assembled laboratory-confirmed data on influenza activity from 1997 to 2005, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They covered the A/H3N2 and A/H1N1 subtypes and influenza B.

The authors describe global patterns in seasonal activity, including viral coexistence and latitudinal gradients, meaning how timing shifts with distance from the equator. Such maps help time vaccination campaigns and anticipate which strains circulate where. The work turns scattered national reports into one comparative picture.
plos-pone-0001396:
Joost Woltering and Antony Durston wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on body plan genes in zebrafish. Hox genes lay out the head to tail axis in animals. Small RNA genes sit inside the Hox clusters too, and they are kept across many species. The pair studied one such RNA, called miR-10, in fish embryos.

The authors show that miR-10 holds back two Hox genes in the fish. By curbing those genes, the small RNA helps set where body parts form. This adds a layer of fine control to the classic Hox plan. It also shows how tiny RNAs shape growth long before the animal takes its final form.
plos-pone-0001496:
Michael Rosenberg and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how muscle like motors build their bundles. Myosin motors form part of the cell's inner frame. Each motor has a long coiled tail, and tails must pack into bundles for the motor to pull at full force. The team asked what steers that packing.

They show the net charge along the tail rod rules both packing and where bundles sit in the cell. Charge is a simple trait with a large effect here. That rule helps labs predict how tail changes will alter cell pull. It may also guide design of man made motor materials.
plos-pone-0001596:
Andrew Kitchen, Michael Miyamoto, and Connie Mulligan wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the Americas were first peopled. They weigh gene, dig, land, and climate proof in one frame. Past tales had split on route and pace. The team set out a three stage model that fits the full proof set.

In their model, a root group first split in Asia. It then waited out the ice age in the far north, then spread south in a swift wave. Each stage rests on a distinct line of proof. A model that honors all lines beats one that picks a favorite. It gives digs and gene hunts a shared map.
plos-pone-0001696:
Pablo Perel and co-authors checked whether clinical trials in Latin America match the region's health needs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Since 1990, non-communicable diseases and injuries have caused most deaths and disability-adjusted life years in Latin America. Trials, though, may cluster on topics of interest to rich countries or drug makers.

The team compared the global burden of disease with randomized clinical trials run in Latin America and published in the five leading medical journals. The full text gives the disease-by-disease comparison and where the gaps fall. A mismatch means research money flows away from the conditions that most shorten and worsen lives in the region.
plos-pone-0001796:
Tianyi Mao, Daniel H. O'Connor, Volker Scheuss, and their co-authors measured a class of glow-based calcium sensors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Genetically encoded calcium indicators, or GECIs, promise to track calcium in chosen neuron groups and even in specific cell compartments. To read their glow as activity, though, users need careful quantitative characterization.

The team characterized a promising GCaMP-type indicator and worked out its subcellular targeting, how to send it to exact cell locations. The full text gives the brightness, speed, and calcium response curves. Calcium imaging is now a workhorse of neuroscience, and papers that calibrate the sensors keep thousands of later experiments honest.
plos-pone-0001896:
Dongkook Park and co-authors mapped hormone-making cells in the fruit fly in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. These cells release peptide signals that steer growth, feeding, and other body tasks. A gene switch called DIMMED, or DIMM, had been tied to how such cells mature in the fly Drosophila.

The team checked two things across the whole fly: which peptide cells carry DIMM, and whether all cells with DIMM make peptides. A full map was still missing. Sorting this out helps labs use the fly to study how hormone cells form and fail. The map also gives a base for work on like cells in other species.
plos-pone-0001996:
Magdalena Zychlinska and co-authors studied a common virus in mouse B cells grown from stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Epstein-Barr virus infects more than ninety-five in a hundred adults and stays in their B cells for life. It is also tied to several cancers, yet it infects human cells in ways mice do not copy easily.

The team made mouse B cells from embryonic stem cells and infected them with the virus. They report that the virus's latent genes, the set it uses while lying low, were expressed only in a restricted way. Limits like this show where mouse models can and cannot stand in for human infection.
plos-pone-0002096:
Charles Rudick and co-authors traced bladder pain to a classic allergy chemical, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mast cells trigger inflammation that comes with local pain, but the steps from cell to pain were unclear. Interstitial cystitis is a bladder disease that causes debilitating pelvic pain of unknown origin. It often shows no consistent inflammation, though its symptoms correlate with mast cell signs.

Leonard W. King published Babylonian Magic and Sorcery in 1896, the first English book on its subject. King edited a series of cuneiform prayers against witchcraft. The leading group is called the Prayers of the Lifting of the Hand.

Babylonians who believed themselves cursed used these rites for relief. The prayers ask gods to break spells, drive off demons, and restore health. King prints transliterations and translations from tablets in the British Museum. Victorian readers could hear ancient Mesopotamia's fears in its own words. The book pioneered the English study of Babylonian ritual texts. Assyriology students still cite its editions.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-7-189:
Thomas Vaughan's Euphrates, or the Waters of the East, fills volume seven of Westcott's series. Vaughan wrote the mystical treatise in 1655 under the name Eugenius Philalethes. Westcott's 1896 reissue adds Florence Farr's full commentary.

Vaughan pours fiery prose on God, nature, and magic into his pages. He attacks dry scholars and defends a living, enchanted philosophy of nature. Farr, the Golden Dawn's leading adept, explains his symbols for modern readers. Her commentary reads seventeenth-century theosophy through nineteenth-century occult eyes. The pairing shows two eras of English mysticism in conversation. Vaughan's twin brother was the poet Henry Vaughan, which adds literary interest.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-8-189:
Florence Farr wrote Egyptian Magic as volume eight of Westcott's Collectanea Hermetica in 1896. Farr was an actress, a Golden Dawn leader, and a serious student of Egypt. She wrote under her order motto, S.S.D.D., in the original edition.

Her handbook treats Egyptian ritual magic from temple texts and museum study. She explains gods, symbols, and invocations in a practical spirit. Farr approached the material as a working magician, not only a scholar. The result is part scholarship and part grimoire in one slim volume. It shows how the Victorian occult revival imagined ancient Egypt. Farr's authority inside the Golden Dawn gave her reading wide influence.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-9-189:
W. Wynn Westcott wrote Numbers: Their Occult Power and Mystic Virtues, first published in 1890. Westcott's Collectanea Hermetica reissued it as volume nine in 1896. The handbook catalogues number symbolism from one upward.

Why is seven lucky and thirteen feared in popular lore? Westcott collects answers from Pythagoras, Kabbalah, astrology, and scripture. Each number receives its virtues, gods, and traditional associations in turn. The Golden Dawn used the book as a pocket reference for symbolism. Compact and endlessly quotable, it served students building rituals and talismans. Westcott's medical day job contrasts oddly with this lore. The handbook still introduces readers to Western numerology.
aubrey-miscellanies-english-1696:
John Aubrey, the great English antiquary, gathered his Miscellanies from a lifetime of notebooks and published them in 1696. Aubrey collected anything curious, and the unseen world drew him strongly. His book gathers apparitions, omens, dreams, second sight, and witchcraft lore from across Britain.

Aubrey reports each case with its place, names, and witnesses, like a clerk of marvels. He neither sneers nor quite swallows; he records. Second sight in Scotland and corpse candles in Wales fill his pages. The result is the folklore of the supernatural from a first-rate collector. Few books show better what educated English folk still believed in 1696.
